title: From the Moog modular to the Behringer System 15
intro: Moog’s modular synthesizers came first: cabinets of separate modules joined by patch cords, used by studios, universities and a few musicians from the mid-1960s. The System 15 was the smallest of the three 1973 systems, a single cabinet of the most useful modules. Behringer’s version copies it in Eurorack size, with a CM1A MIDI module instead of the Moog keyboard.

timeline.name: The first Moog modules
timeline.text: Robert Moog, working with the composer Herb Deutsch, builds oscillators and amplifiers whose pitch and level are set by a control voltage. One module can now play another, and pitch follows 1 V per octave: the idea every module on this panel is built on.

timeline.name: Complete Moog systems
timeline.text: Moog starts selling ready-made cabinets of modules, the Synthesizers I, II and III. The 900-series modules on this panel (921 oscillators, 904 filters, 902 amplifiers, 911 envelopes) are the ones they were built from.

timeline.name: Switched-On Bach
timeline.text: Wendy Carlos’s album of Bach played on a Moog modular, one line at a time, becomes a hit and makes “Moog” the word for a synthesizer.

timeline.name: System 15, System 35, System 55
timeline.text: Moog replaces its older systems with three new sizes: the System 15 in one portable cabinet, the System 35, and the large System 55 with the 960 sequencer. The modules are the same 900 series, arranged differently.

timeline.name: Moog’s own reissues
timeline.text: Moog Music rebuilds the System 55, the System 35 and the Model 15 in small numbers from the original documents, by hand and at a high price.

timeline.name: Behringer’s 900 series
timeline.text: Behringer recreates the modules in Eurorack size, sold singly and as the System 15, System 35 and System 55, at a fraction of the cost of an original. A CM1A MIDI-to-CV module stands in for the Moog keyboard.

timeline.name: Behringer System 15
timeline.text: Sixteen modules in two rows: the 921A driver with two 921B oscillators, a 921, the 904A, 904B, 914 and 923 filters, two 902 amplifiers, two 911 envelopes, the CP3A-M mixer, the CP35 attenuators, the 961 interface and the CM1A.

relatives.name: Minimoog Model D
relatives.text: The same ideas fixed into one portable instrument with no patch cords: three oscillators, the ladder filter and two envelopes. The Behringer Model D, its copy, is in this app.

relatives.name: ARP 2500
relatives.text: Moog’s rival in large studio modulars, connected with matrix switches instead of patch cords. Its smaller sibling, the 2600, is in this app.

relatives.name: Buchla 100 series
relatives.text: Don Buchla’s modular, built at the same time on the American west coast, with different ideas: no keyboard, sequencers and low-pass gates. The Buchla Music Easel in this app comes from it.

note: The records listed are ones where a Moog modular is well documented. The Moog systems differed in size, not in their modules, so a record made on any Moog modular is listed here. The sounds they link to are only in that style.
